Figure 2: Colaroid implements code versioning and change propagating through git. Suppose the author wants to edit the first
step (e.g., changing HTML page title) and propagate the change to subsequent steps. Colaroid maps steps with the hash ID of
the code commits in Git. As shown in phase 1 and phase 2, Colaroid will first check out the main branch into a new branch
named “change” and reset the head to the code version that needs to be edited. By doing this, authors would see commit A
loaded in their code editor. Next, tutorial authors can make changes directly in the code editor. Once they confirm finishing the
edits, Colaroid will create a new commit for the changes and merge commits in the later steps into the change branch.

figures.proposed_alt: Five-phase diagram of propagating a tutorial edit through Git. Initially the main branch contains commits A and B. Colaroid creates a change branch at A, the author edits A to make A-prime, and later changes are reapplied to produce B-prime. The final phase removes the original main branch and renames change to main. Tutorial step entries are updated to the new commit IDs so the edited page title propagates to later steps.

figures.current_alt: Figure 3 is a complex system diagram depicting the interface between the Arbility tool and the Arboretum architecture. The Arbility tool consists of a chat interface (A) and a Chromium web browser (B). The Arboretum architecture consists of a web server (C) and a mirroring module (D). The blind end user interacts with the Arbility chat interface by inputting messages, which are sent to the Arboretum web server and forwarded to sighted crowd workers. These crowd workers then send proposed actions and events back to the Arboretum server, which forwards them to the end user for acceptance or rejection. If the end user accepts the events, the corresponding page updates are executed in the Arbility Chromium browser, which then sends these changes to the Arboretum mirroring module. The mirroring module then syncs these changes with the Arboretum web server so that the updates due to the accepted action are also visible to remote crowd workers. The diagram depicts these components and their interactions as labeled boxes with directed arrows between them.

figures.current_alt: This figure illustrates the process of generalizing a parameter XPath from the unique XPath string for original value "Apple" to a generalized XPath formula to match all values for the "fruit" parameter. The first line of the figure is the unique XPath "html > ... > .section[1] > .fruit[1] > div[1] > span[2]", which matches the text "Apple" only. An arrow is then drawn to the next line, "html > ... > .section[1] > .fruit[1] > div[index] > span[2]", where "div[1]" is generalized to "div[index]", which results in this XPath now matching the text "Apple", "Banana", and "Pineapple". Finally, an arrow is drawn from this second line to the third/last line, "html > ... > .section[1] > .fruit[1] > div[index] > span.description", where "span[2]" is generalized to "span.description", resulting in the final generalized XPath formula which matches "Apple", "Banana", "Pineapple", and now "Fig" too.

figures.current_alt: Figure 2. Network summarizing commonly reported debugging strategy transitions from 16 expert web developers. It is a descriptive model, not a decision tree: context questions do not uniquely determine the next strategy, and a missing edge does not rule out a transition. Six green ellipses are numbered: 1, Forward-reasoning; 2, Error-message; 3, Hypothesis-test; 4, Backward-reasoning; 5, Simplification; and 6, External Strategy. Starting from whether a defect is observable, the diagram connects a non-observable defect through codebase complexity (l) to forward reasoning. For an observable defect, clear messages (a) lead toward error-message debugging, vague messages (b) toward hypothesis testing, and client-side versus other failures (c) toward simplification or hypothesis testing. Error-message debugging connects through access to the codebase (d) to backward reasoning. Hypothesis testing connects through debugger availability (e) to backward reasoning, or through reproducibility (f), familiarity (g), and search-space size (h) to simplification. Constrained production, compiled-binary, or ownership contexts (i) distinguish external strategies from simplification. User-specific failures (j) also connect hypothesis testing to external strategies. Sporadic behavior or infeasible traces (k) connect backward reasoning back to hypothesis testing; legacy or unmaintained code (n) connects to backward reasoning. Forward reasoning connects through familiarity (m) toward hypothesis testing when familiar or external strategies when unfamiliar, and through reproducibility and a narrowed search space (o) toward simplification. Simplification connects through unsafe or limited opportunities to simplify (q) toward external strategies. Context boxes are blue for codebase characteristics, tan for defect characteristics, and pale yellow for environmental, tooling, and organizational constraints. The printed legend labels both codebase and defect characteristics as Table IV; the body text identifies codebase characteristics in Table V. Arrow weight encodes breadth of participant support: thick solid lines, at least 7 participants; thin solid lines, 4 to 6; dashed lines, 3 or fewer. Thick routes emphasize complexity to forward reasoning, clear errors to error-message debugging, debugger availability to backward reasoning, familiarity to hypothesis testing, and a large search space to simplification. Dashed routes include reproducible, narrowed problems from forward reasoning to simplification, sporadic or infeasible traces from backward reasoning to hypothesis testing, and unsafe simplification to external strategies. Table VII gives the associated conditions, participant evidence, and quotations.

Figure 1 presents an illustration of four different keyframes created in Expresso for a sample web page.
Each keyframe is a rectangle of a different shape and size, representing different viewport sizes.
The four keyframes appear as though on an x-axis, sorted by viewport width, with the narrowest keyframe on the left and the widest keyframe on the right.
There is a bi-directional arrow above the set of keyframes with the label 'viewport width', providing a label for the axis. 
The sample web page shown in the keyframes is adapted from the Mozilla website that we used during one of our study tasks.
Each keyframe has the following items: 1) a blue background, 2) the orange FireFox logo, 3) the text 'The new Firefox' in white font, 4) the text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in white font, 5) a green rectangle representing a button, with the text 'Download Firefox' on it in white font, and 6) an illustration of an open laptop with a Firefox browser shown.
Note that the element and viewport widths mentioned below are not to scale; the keyframes are shrunk down for the figure.
Moving from left to right, the keyframes can be described as follows:
The leftmost keyframe is called k_0 and has a width of 722 pixels. The viewport width is narrow compared to its height, and represents the portrait-view viewport on a mobile device. In keyframe k_0, the whole web page has a blue background. The other elements on the page are all horizontally centered and stacked vertically. At the top is the Firefox logo which is medium-sized. Below that is the text 'The new Firefox' in a small font size. Below that is the text 'Fast for good.' in a large font size. Below that is the long line of text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in a very small font size. Below that is the green 'Download Firefox' button. Below that is the laptop illustration which is of medium size and which is at the bottom of the page. Note that the laptop's x-position is 148 pixels.
The next keyframe is called k_1 and has a width of 990 pixels. The viewport width is approximately the same as the viewport height. In keyframe k_1, the UI elements have the same arrangement as in k_0, with all elements horizontally centered and stacked vertically. All elements are the same size as in k_0. Since k_1's viewport is wider, there is more margin to the left and right of elements. Note that the laptop's x-position is 203 pixels.
The next keyframe is called k_2 and has a width of 1000 pixels. The viewport width is wider than the viewport height. In k_2, the page has the same elements as in k_0 and k_1, but a vastly different layout and some elements are different sizes. k_2 has more of a 2-column layout.  In k_2, the blue background only takes up the top half of the page (the lower half of the page is a placeholder gray). The Firefox logo is smaller and is on the far-left edge of the page. The 'The new Firefox' text is of medium font size and appear directly to the right of the Firefox logo. Below the 'The new Firefox' text appears the 'Fast for good' text of large font size. Below that is the long line of text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in a very small font size. Below that is the green button with the text 'Download Firefox'. The text elements and the green button are left-aligned with each other. On the right side of the screen is the laptop, of large size, with equal margin on its left and right sides. Note that the laptop's x-position is 550 pixels.
The next keyframe is called k_3 and has a width of 1200 pixels. The viewport width is much wider than the viewport height. In k_3, the UI elements have the same 2-column arrangement as in k_2. The only difference is that, with the wider page size, the laptop has more margin on its left and right sides. Note that the laptop's x-position is 650 pixels.
As a summary of the layouts, keyframes k_0 and k_1 have all elements horizontally centered and stacked vertically. k_2 and k_3 have the Firefox logo and all text on the left side of the page, and the laptop on the right side of the page.
Each keyframe has a colored-strip beneath it to help in explaining transitions between keyframes. k_0 has a light green strip, k_1 has a magenta strip, k_2 has a turquoise strip, and k_3 has a brown strip.
Each strip also has a label of the laptop's x-position on it, as the transitions highlighted in this figure are those for the laptop x-position.
There is a colored-strip between each pair of adjacent keyframes representing the transition type.
The colored-strip between k_0 and k_1 is a left-to-right gradient of light green to magenta, indicating a smooth transition between k_0 and k_1.
Similarly, the colored-strip between k_2 and k_3 is a left-to-right gradient, of turquoise to light brown, indicating a smooth transition between k_2 and k_3.
The colored-strip between k_1 (magenta) and k_2 (turquoise) is a solid color of magent indicating a jump transition between k_1 and k_2. Specifically, the magenta color means that the range between k_1 and k_2, namely viewport sizes 991 to 999 pixels, should continue the behavior for the laptop x-position from the smaller viewports. This means that the laptop (and all UI elements) are shown horizontally centered and stacked vertically for the range of viewports 991 to 999 pixels wide.
There are range arrows below the set of keyframes indicating the laptop x-position. Figure 2: Overview of the three conflict-free mechanisms in
PADLOCK. (A) Cell-level access control allows collaborators
to claim ownership of the code cells and restrict others from
editing or viewing them: (A1) Unchecking edit access for a
user will change the cell background and disable editing;
(A2) Unchecking read access for a user will blur the cell. (B)
Variable-level access control extends the idea of access con-
trol from cells to shared variables: (B1) Unchecking a user’s
variable access; (B2) After losing access, they will not be able
to edit the variable and will receive warning when attempt-
ing to do so. (C) Parallel cell groups define a designated area
where changes of the code and runtime state stay inside its
own scope: (C1) One parallel cell group can contain multiple
tabs; (C2) Each tab can contain multiple cells; (C3) Sync the
variables from the global scope to the current active tab; (C4)
Add a new tab; (C5) Click the radio button to mark it as the
“main” tab.

Figure 1: CFlow allows users to explore the semantic flows of student code submissions at a high level through semantic
aggregation. First, users are presented with an overview of the entire set of solutions (1), including the SAV (a) and the SHV
(b). They can then click on individual code lines (f) to progressively explore the details of specific implementations. The
visualization will update to focus on a smaller subset of solutions, displaying the aggregated flow and distributions of the
selected set only (2). Users can inspect details of the flow at individual code level in the CDV (e). CFlow offers a breakdown of
types of errors within that group (k), and detailed solutions with context-aware highlighting (h).

keeps the current value but gets rid of the constraints that were in place when the user
